title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Guided and Individualized, Web-Based, Stress Management Program for Stressed Managers
abstract: Purpose: Occupational stress is a common health issue and it causes significant problems for many individuals and rehabilitation of stress is costly to society. A substantial part of the total costs of stress and stress related disorders are due to work absenteeism, work impairment, and loss of work productivity. Occupational stress appears to be especially frequent among low and mid-level managers. Research has shown that web-based behavioral health programs are effective for treating anxiety, depression and other health related issues. These programs increase accessibility of evidence-based interventions to individuals who are not able or willing to receive such in-person treatments. Stress management training has empirical support, but little data exists on its efficacy with stressed managers when delivered via the internet. In light of these observations we are currently conducting a randomized controlled trial of a guided and individualized, web-based, stress management program (iSTRESS) for stressed managers.Methods: The participants are recruited by self-referral through advertisement in national newspapers and on the internet. The main inclusion criterion was stress as a primary diagnosis. Participants with comorbid diagnosis (anxiety, depression, insomnia) were also included as long as the stress diagnosis was considered primary. We aim to include a total of 100 participants and randomize them into two groups (iSTRESS or an attention control group) that will discuss stress-related topics in a web-based and moderated forum. Both programs will last for eight weeks and all participants will received a weekly mail contact with a psychologist. Participants will be evaluated on self-report measures, for stress (PSS), burnout (SMBQ), depression (MADRS), anxiety (BAI), insomnia (ISI) and other health-related issues. We will also measure health-economic aspects, such as: absenteeism, use of medication, and care.Results: Analyses will be based on both study completers and intention to treat. Final pre-post treatment results will be available in December and 3 month follow-up in March 2014. Preliminary result from a previous small sample pilot (n=8) trail on the iSTRESS-program showed promising results on measures of stress at post-assessment (7 points improvement on the Perceived Stress Scale, pre=25).Conclusions: To our knowledge this is the first controlled trail examining the efficacy of a web-based stress management program for managers. Final pre-post and 3 month follow-up treatment results will be available for presentation at the EAOHP 2014 conference.

title: Evaluating a Digital Mindful Self-Compassion Intervention to Reduce Compassion Fatigue in Violence Service Workers: A Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Compassion Fatigue (CF) often occurs among violence service workers, who face victims of violence daily, making them vulnerable to emotional exhaustion, decreased empathy, and burnout. This phenomenon not only affects their personal quality of life but also has the potential to reduce the quality of service they provide. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a digital intervention using the Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC) approach in reducing compassion fatigue among violence case service workers. The research design is a randomized controlled pilot study with a total of 25 participants randomly divided into two groups: intervention (n=12) and wait-list control (n=13). The intervention was conducted over six sessions across six weeks, combining Zoom sessions, self-paced materials accessed via a website, and a WhatsApp group. CF was measured using the Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQol-V), mindfulness using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS), and self-compassion using the Self-Compassion Scale (SCS), which has been adapted into Indonesian. The study results showed that the MSC intervention significantly reduced CF in the intervention group compared to the control group. Specifically, CF scores in the intervention group decreased from a pre-test mean of 57.17 to a post-test mean of 48.17, t(11) = 3.270, p = .007, indicating a statistically significant improvement. Meanwhile, the control group did not experience a significant change (p = .662). Between-group analysis at post-test confirmed a significant difference favoring the intervention group, t = -2.573, p = .017. In addition to the reduction in CF, mindfulness scores significantly increased in the intervention group from 56.67 to 61.92 (p = .009), and the common humanity subscale of self-compassion showed a notable improvement (p = .031). These results suggest that the digital MSC program effectively enhanced emotional resilience and mitigated compassion fatigue symptoms among trauma-exposed service providers. Qualitative feedback from participants indicated significant benefits from social support during the sessions and the accessibility of materials through the website. MSC intervention is effective in improving the psychological well-being of violence case service workers, thus the widespread implementation of the MSC program in this work environment is highly recommended to enhance mental health and service quality.

title: Effect of a Brief Intervention Program on Burnout among Medical Students at Faculty of Medicine in Suez Canal University, Egypt
abstract: Background: Studies revealed that stress and burnout developed in medical students during their academic learning years, progress throughout their clinical years, and proceed in their practice as physicians. This can negatively impact their learning abilities, mental, cognitive, and physical health.Therefore, effective programs are needed to assure medical students’ well-being, and to prevent negative consequences of burnout and stress related to medical training. Aim: This study was aiming to improve the provided care to medical students by improving their mental and psychological health by providing baseline information on the prevalence of stress and burnout and by conducting an interventional program to reduce them. Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted on medical students in the Faculty of Medicine, Suez Canal University, Egypt. Socio-demographic questionnaire was used to collect data in addition to the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBI-SS) to measure burnout, and the General Health Questionnaire-12 (GHQ-12) to measure stress. The intervention group and control group contained 50 students per each, where randomization was done using the computerized method. The program was a 3-day workshop with a post-test followed it by 1 month. Results: The prevalence of stress among students was 51%, while that of burnout was 43%. After implementing the program there was a significant improvement in the scores of emotional exhaustion (EE), academic performance domain of burnout, and GHQ-12 among the intervention group. Conclusion:Brief intervention programs can help students to cope with their stress leading to significant improvements and a decrease in the prevalence of burnout among them.

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Longitudinal Mindfulness Intervention to Decrease Burnout in Medical Residents
abstract:
Introduction: Burnout is common among resident physicians due to the emotional, intellectual, and time demands of training. Mind-body interventions such as mindfulness may alleviate stress and protect against burnout.
Methods: A randomized controlled longitudinal mindfulness intervention was implemented in both internal medicine and pediatrics residency programs for first-year residents at Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, MO). This included three 30-minute mindfulness training sessions and encouragement to use the smartphone application, Insight Timer. Primary outcomes were baseline and 12 month burnout scores, measured by Maslach Burnout Inventory. Secondary outcomes assessed feasibility and individual mindfulness practice during the study period. Analysis was performed utilizing paired t-tests to matched pre and post-intervention data as well as multivariate regression analysis to discover possible associations with burnout.
Results: Twenty-four residents (24/69 (35%) of those randomized) completed both surveys and were included in the analysis. Emotional exhaustion scores improved in the intervention group but worsened in the control, with a mean score difference of -3.1 vs 2.0, respectively, but did not achieve statistical significance (p=0.244). Depersonalization scores increased (worsened) in both groups, but less so in the intervention group (mean score difference 0.8 vs 3.1, p=0.412). A majority of residents in both groups agreed they benefited from regular practice of mindfulness (intervention: 11/17 [65%]; control: 12/16 [75%], p=0.712). Most of residents agreed (7/17, 41%) or felt neutral (8/17, 47%) that the intervention was useful throughout the year.
Conclusions: This randomized controlled trial of a longitudinal mindfulness intervention in residents proved easy to implement, affordable, and resulted a trend towards improved burnout scores in the intervention arm Residency programs and healthcare organizations can adopt similar strategies to improve physician mental health and reduce burnout.

title: Online Mindfulness Training and Work-related Outcomes: A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Trial
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of an online mindfulness training program, "Mindfulness for Humans" (MfH), on key work-related outcomes among private sector employees in the United States. Mindfulness is defined as “the awareness that emerges through paying attention on purpose, in the present moment, and nonjudgmentally to the unfolding of experience moment by moment” (Kabat-Zinn, 2003). Extensive research has documented its benefits for reducing anxiety, depression, stress, and substance dependence, while improving emotional regulation, decision-making, prosocial behavior, and certain physiological markers (e.g., cortisol levels and brain activity in areas related to problem-solving and emotion regulation). Despite growing corporate interest in mindfulness programs (e.g., at Google, Aetna, General Mills, and Target), empirical evidence remains limited regarding their specific impact on workplace outcomes such as job satisfaction, job burnout, and work engagement—particularly among private sector employees. Most existing studies and meta-analyses focus on public sector occupations (e.g., healthcare and education workers), general well-being, or stress reduction rather than work-specific outcomes. Private sector jobs comprise approximately 85% of U.S. employment, yet findings from public sector samples may not fully generalize due to differences in job demands, contexts, and organizational structures. This randomized waitlist-controlled trial addresses these gaps by evaluating whether a standardized online mindfulness intervention can improve job satisfaction, reduce burnout, increase work engagement, enhance mindfulness skills, and boost subjective well-being in a private sector sample. Study Purpose and Design The primary purpose is to test the causal effects of the MfH program on these outcomes using a rigorous experimental design. The study employs an adapted randomized crossover (waitlist control) design with two groups and three assessment timepoints (pre-test, mid-test after 30 days, and post-test after 60 days total). Group A receives immediate access to the MfH course during the first 30 day period, followed by a 30 day wait period. Group B serves as the waitlist control during the first 30 day, then receives access to the course during the second 30 day period. This design allows within- and between-group comparisons to evaluate intervention effects while providing all participants eventual access to the training. Participants complete the same battery of validated self-report measures at each timepoint via Qualtrics. Course engagement is tracked objectively as the percentage of the 15-session program completed. The Intervention: Mindfulness for Humans (MfH) MfH is a 15-session, self-paced online mindfulness training program (approximately 20–25 minutes per session). Each lesson includes: A brief “arrive” introductory video (1–2 minutes) with a poem or quote and nature imagery. An instructional video (5–7 minutes) on the session topic. A guided mindfulness practice (15–20 minutes). The course provides roughly 2 hours of didactic content and 4 hours of guided practice. Content is empirically grounded in the mindfulness literature and delivered by an instructor with over 10 years of formal training in mindfulness-based interventions. Lesson topics cover foundational concepts (e.g., what mindfulness is, taming the mind), working with emotions and thoughts, compassion and self-compassion, gratitude, impermanence, resilience, relationships, interconnectedness, and cultivating joy/peace. Key Outcomes and Measures Primary work-related outcomes: Job Satisfaction — measured with the Job Satisfaction Survey (JSS) composite score. Job Burnout — measured with the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (OLBI) overall score. Work Engagement — measured with the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale-9 (UWES-9) overall score. Secondary outcomes: Mindfulness — assessed with the 15-item Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ-15) total score and the My Best Self 101 Mindfulness Questionnaire (MBS101-MQ), the latter also serving as a psychometric validation opportunity. Subjective Well-Being — measured with the Survey on Flourishing. Additional data include demographics (age, sex, race, education, industry, job tenure, salary, etc.), prior mindfulness experience, and post-intervention feedback on course satisfaction, perceived work impacts, and likelihood of continued practice. Hypotheses Within-person improvement: Job satisfaction, work engagement, mindfulness, and subjective well-being will increase (and burnout will decrease) from pre- to post-intervention after completing the MfH course. Between-group difference: After the first 4-week period, Group A (immediate intervention) will show greater improvements than Group B (waitlist control). Group B is expected to show comparable gains during their subsequent intervention period. Exploratory: Greater engagement with the MfH course (percentage completed) will be associated with larger improvements in the outcomes. Expected Outcomes and Contributions We expect the MfH program to produce small-to-medium positive effects on the targeted outcomes, consistent with prior meta-analyses of workplace mindfulness training, while providing stronger evidence for private sector employees. By using a fully online, standardized intervention with objective engagement tracking, the study minimizes heterogeneity common in prior research and enhances accessibility and replicability. This research will contribute to the literature by: Filling the gap in private sector mindfulness research. Providing rigorous evidence on work-specific outcomes (job satisfaction, burnout, and engagement) beyond general well-being. Evaluating an accessible, scalable online program that organizations could readily adopt. Offering preliminary psychometric data on the MBS101-MQ. Findings could inform corporate wellness initiatives, helping employers support employee mental health and performance without replacing necessary organizational-level changes. The study does not promote mindfulness as a sole “quick fix” for systemic workplace issues but examines its potential role within broader support strategies. The target sample for the study is 160 participants entering the study with the expectation of retaining 120 through the study, based on a 33% attrition rate. Sample sized was determined based on a power analysis with g ≈ .30, f = .15, and power = .80. Planned analysis for the study will involve mixed-effects models for repeated measures using maximum likelihood estimation in Stata. Data screening, outlier handling, and demographic checks will follow standard procedures.

title: Efficacy of an Online Mindfulness Training to Improve Well-Being in K-12 Teachers: A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Trial
abstract: Concerns about the mental health and well-being of K-12 schoolteachers have never been more urgent, with stress levels, burnout, and rates of attrition reaching historically high levels. Mindfulness-based interventions may be a professional development option for teachers to better meet the demands of their career with skills such as mental flexibility, emotion regulation, resilience, empathy, compassion, and interpersonal skills. This study examines the efficacy of the Mindfulness for Humans (MfH) course, an online, self-directed mindfulness curriculum that is grounded in evidence-based practices, is easily accessible and scalable, relatively brief, and requires little or no work on the part of the school system to implement. This study utilized a randomized waitlist-controlled trial to examine the feasibility and impact of the MfH course on the well-being and mindfulness skills of 230 K-12 teachers of regular classrooms using responses to self-report measures and qualitative responses to a satisfaction questionnaire. Evidence suggested that online mindfulness training through the MfH course significantly increases teacher well-being and mindfulness skills, regardless of initial familiarity with the topic of mindfulness, and is engaging and useful to them. Online mindfulness training through the MfH course may support the well-being of K-12 schoolteachers. Future research may examine additional outcomes such as teacher stress, resilience, or psychological distress.

title: Mental and physical training with meditation and aerobic exercise improved mental health and well-being in teachers during the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Teachers face significant stressors in relation to their work, placing them at increased risk for burnout and attrition. The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about additional challenges, resulting in an even greater burden. Thus, strategies for reducing stress that can be delivered virtually are likely to benefit this population. Mental and Physical (MAP) Training combines meditation with aerobic exercise and has resulted in positive mental and physical health outcomes in both clinical and subclinical populations. The aim of this pilot study was to evaluate the feasibility and potential effectiveness of virtual MAP Training on reducing stress and improving mood and well-being in teachers. Participants (n= 104) were from recruited online from kindergarten to grade twelve (K-12) schools in the Northeastern region of the United States and randomly assigned to a 6-week program of virtual MAP Training (n= 58) or no training (n= 13). Primary outcomes included pre-intervention and post-intervention ratings on self-report measures of social and emotional health. Changes in cognitive functioning and physical health were also examined in secondary analyses. By intervention end, participants in the MAP Training group reported less anxiety and work-related stress compared to those who received no training (ds = −0.75 to −0.78). Additionally, MAP Training participants reported improvements in depressive symptoms, rumination, work-related quality of life, perceived stress, and self-compassion (ds = 0.38 to −0.82), whereas no changes were observed in the no training group. Participants also reported increased subjective ratings of executive functioning, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and fewer sleep disturbances (ds = −0.41 to −0.74). Together, these results suggest that the combination of meditation and aerobic exercise is an effective virtual intervention for improving mental health and well-being among K-12 teachers and may enhance resilience to stressful life events such as occurred during the coronavirus pandemic.

title: AIZEN Digital Meditation Intervention for Caregiver Burnout in Taiwan—A Pilot Randomized Trial
abstract: Caregiver stress is a global health issue, particularly acute in Taiwan due to demographic and cultural factors. While mindfulness meditation is effective for burnout, research on culturally adapted, digitally delivered interventions for Taiwanese caregivers is lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a brief, 5-week, digitally supported meditation program for professional and informal caregivers in Taiwan. We conducted a randomized, stratified, wait-list control trial with 57 meditation-naïve caregivers (42 professional, 15 informal). The intervention combined weekly live online sessions with daily guided practice via the AIZEN digital platform. Primary outcomes for professionals were personal, work-related, and client-related burnout, measured by the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory. The secondary outcome for informal caregivers was burden, measured by the Zarit Burden Interview. Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T1), post-intervention (T2), and 5-week follow-up (T3). Compared to the wait-list group, the immediate-intervention professional caregivers showed significantly greater reductions from T1 to T2 in personal burnout ( β = 12.50, p = 0.011) and work-related burnout ( β = 11.43, p = 0.015). The effect on work-related burnout was replicated in the primary analysis and maintained at follow-up, though this lost significance in a sensitivity analysis. No significant effects were found for client-related burnout or informal caregiver burden. A brief, digitally supported mindfulness meditation program is a feasible, effective approach for reducing personal and work-related burnout among professional caregivers in Taiwan. These findings support the implementation of scalable digital mental health tools and warrant investigation in larger trials. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07188454.

title: BiWell: Bicocca + Workplace Well-being. An effectiveness analysis of a smartphone app for managing stress and promoting well-being at work
abstract: In today’s work environment, stress is recognised as one of the main risk factors for the onset of various psycho-physical disorders. It is well known that perceived stress can lead to the development of symptoms such as depression, anxiety, and behavioural problems. Organisations can play a key role in preventing employee psycho-physical health issues by reaching out during times of need and offering effective interventions. The widespread use of new technologies among the general population and within organisational contexts has proven to be an ally in planning and managing such interventions—particularly through the use of smartphones and related mobile applications. These tools have made the delivery of stress management interventions easier and more accessible. The World Health Organization defines mobile health (m-health) as all health practices and tools supported by mobile devices, such as smartphones and other wireless devices, aimed at monitoring and promoting health and well-being. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of smartphone-based interventions, not only in clinical settings but also in educational and academic contexts. While digital technologies offer numerous advantages—such as access to interventions anytime and anywhere, reduced stigma associated with seeking mental health support, personalisation, accessibility, and cost-effectiveness—they also present several limitations that can hinder their effectiveness and user engagement. The main challenges include a lack of theoretical foundations guiding intervention design, high dropout rates, privacy concerns, and low user engagement—an essential prerequisite for effectiveness. As part of the MUSA (Multilayered Urban Sustainability Action) project, Spoke 2, WP3 “Big Data and Innovative Approaches to Improve Global Health and Well-being,” funded by the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), and in collaboration with the Bicocca Center for Applied Psychology, BiWell was developed—a smartphone application for managing work-related stress and promoting well-being. BiWell allows users to engage in daily exercises tailored to their reported emotional state at each login. Each exercise includes content based on techniques and practices aimed at enhancing personal resources and developing coping strategies for stress management and well-being. The exercises are grounded in principles of positive psychology, mindfulness, self-compassion, and physical activation. The research is a longitudinal randomised controlled trial (RCT) with two conditions (intervention group and active control group). Participants will be asked to use BiWell for 8 weeks. Additionally, a follow-up will be conducted 8 weeks after the end of the intervention to assess the stability of the outcomes over time. The aim of this research project is to evaluate the effectiveness of digital interventions—specifically those delivered through BiWell—and to analyse related usage patterns among workers. To evaluate effectiveness, we plan to compare the intervention group (participants who can access the app and unlock the daily exercise) with an active control group (participants who can access the app and report their daily emotional state but cannot unlock any exercises). We expect that participants in the intervention group will report a significant reduction in job burnout and stress, as well as a significant increase in subjective well-being and psychological capital, compared to the active control group. Additionally, we expect that app access and usage data can predict effectiveness (e.g. higher app use should predict a higher decrease in negative symptoms and a higher increase in positive outcomes). During the study period, we will also assess the perceived usability and user engagement of BiWell, as previous literature suggests these factors are strongly related to an app’s effectiveness. We expect that higher ratings of usability and engagement will predict greater intervention effectiveness. We are also interested in exploring the possible effects of covariates and moderators on principal outcomes. We also plan to conduct some exploratory analysis using self-monitoring data aimed at (1) exploring possible relationships between perceived well-being and patterns of mobile app usage; (2) investigating potential patterns between daily affectivity and the effectiveness of the intervention. Lastly, we are interested in exploring whether the user profiles identified in previous research will be replicated, and whether the intervention's effectiveness will differ based on these profiles. If the profiles are confirmed, we expect significant differences in effectiveness across user types.

title: Edu:Social School Study: Promoting well-being and socio-emotional competencies for school teachers with App-based Mindfulness and Dyad-based empathy-compassion trainings.
abstract: The teaching profession is widely recognized as highly demanding, and teachers report elevated rates of stress and burnout (García-Carmona et al., 2019; Iriarte Redín & Erro-Garcés, 2020). If left unaddressed, burnout adversely affects teachers’ health, job performance, teaching quality, and school turnover rates (Bellingrath et al., 2009; García-Carmona et al., 2019; Madigan & Kim, 2021). Moreover, teacher burnout has important consequences for students. Teachers’ emotional exhaustion has been shown to negatively affect students’ academic achievement and self-concept in Germany (Klusmann et al., 2016, 2022). Given teachers’ pivotal role in shaping children's socio-emotional development, addressing psychological vulnerability—including stress, depression, anxiety, loneliness, and exhaustion—is essential. Strengthening resilience enables teachers to maintain well-being and effective classroom functioning in the face of adversity by supporting adaptive stress management (Gu & Day, 2013). In addition, strong interpersonal skills such as empathy, compassion and high-quality listening quality play an important role in the teacher-student communication (Wolvin & Coakley, 2000). Addressing psychological vulnerability and strengthening resilience and social capacities, is essential not only for teacher well-being but also for the functioning of educational systems broadly (García-Carmona et al., 2019; Madigan & Kim, 2021). Mindfulness-based interventions (MBI’s) have emerged as promising approaches for reducing stress and psychological vulnerability while simultaneously strengthening resilience and socio-emotional capacities (for a review, see Singer, 2025). Mindfulness- and compassion-based interventions (Kirby et al., 2017; Klingbeil & Renshaw, 2018; Zarate et al., 2019) as well as social-emotional learning programs (Jennings et al., 2017; Oliveira et al., 2021), have shown encouraging results in reducing teacher stress, exhaustion and burnout. These programs aim to cultivate mindfulness, compassion toward oneself and others, resilience, and proactive stress management among teachers (Kirby et al., 2017; Klingbeil & Renshaw, 2018; Oliveira et al., 2021). However, the literature remains inconclusive regarding which specific components of these interventions are most effective, as many programs combine multiple contemplative practices, making difficult to isolate their distinct effects (Klingbeil & Renshaw, 2018; Zarate et al., 2019). In recent years, classic MBI’s focusing on mental practices done alone, have been further developed to also include social practices done with a partner, so-called Contemplative Dyads (Kok & Singer, 2017), in particular to improve social skills such as empathy, (self-)compassion, and social cohesion (for a review, see Singer, 2025). Current evidence indicates that these social practice formats may be more effective than classic solitary mindfulness practices in reducing loneliness and social stress, strengthening social connection and cohesion, and enhancing resilience and optimism—factors associated with improved psychological functioning (Matthäus et al., 2024a; Matthäus et al., 2024b; Godara, et al., 2021; Godara et al., 2024). Moreover, findings suggest that the mechanisms underlying dyadic social practices differ from those of traditional mindfulness-based interventions (Godara et al., 2024; Singer, 2025). In a previous large-scale 9-month longitudinal mental training study, the ReSource project (Singer et al., 2015) the differential effects of different types of practice modules on mind, brain and body were established suggesting that it really “mattered what you practice” (for a review see, Singer & Engert, 2019). In a follow-up, low-dose purely online mental training study, the CovSocial project (Godara et al., 2021) the partner-based Affect Dyad (Kok & Singer, 2017b), firstly introduced into the Affect module of the ReSource project together with other core meditations, was directly compared with a comparable classic mindfulness training (for a review, see Singer, 2025). Results showed that a 10-week online socio-emotional Dyadic as compared to a mindfulness training differed in their effects as well as the underlying mechanisms (Singer, 2025). Although both trainings could improve mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety and emotion regulation difficulties as well as compassion, they also showed unique effects in that the socio-emotional Dyad training was more efficient to boost resilience, positivity bias, social connectedness and reduce loneliness and social stress on the hormonal level. Further, common effects were shown to rely on partly distinct psychological mechanisms, indicating that mindfulness practices done alone and social Dyad practices may impact well-being through different pathways (Godara et al., 2021; Godara et al., 2024; Godara & Singer, 2024a, 2024b; Matthäus et al., 2024a; Matthäus et al., 2024b; Silveira et al., 2023; for an overview see: Singer, 2025). Attention-based mindfulness practices primarily improved attentional control, present-moment awareness, and interoceptive processes. Further, they reduced rumination, personal distress (empathic distress), and worry, and thus seem to work primarily through changing reflective and attention-based networks in the brain (see also Valk et al., 2015) and stabilizing and calming the mind. In contrast, partner-based socio-emotional Dyad practices seem to work through activating the so-called care-system (Singer & Engert, 2019, Singer, 2025) and by this, strengthen social competencies such as empathy, compassion, and social connectedness as well as resilience and positive affect and resources (Kok & Singer, 2017; Silveira et al., 2023; Singer, 2025). The socio-emotional Affect Dyad intervention is specifically designed to cultivate social capacities such as empathy and (self-)compassion. Evidence indicates, however, that healthy empathy can also turn into empathic distress, especially when one is vulnerable oneself and confronted with strong others’ suffering whereas compassion has been shown to be more resilient and protective in coping with suffering as it is based on altruistic and care-based motivational systems associated with positive affect (Singer & Klimecki, 2014). Empathy and compassion rely on distinct psychological and neuronal mechanisms, with compassion engaging regulatory processes that help buffer emotional overwhelm and support resilience (Klimecki et al., 2014, 2013; Singer & Klimecki, 2014). Given the central role teachers play in students’ academic and socio-emotional development, the ability to distinguish between these crucial social emotions and know how to engage in empathic or compassionate listening may constitute a crucial professional skill in educational contexts. Thus, in the context of a first pilot study, the Edu:Social School Pilot study, the lab developed a so-called EmCo training program (Empathy-Compassion), in which the Affect Dyad based 10-week socio-emotional online program of the CovSocial Project, was expanded in adding an empathy and compassion listening component. In this initial Edu:Social School pilot study 120 teachers were engaged and trained in a 10-week socio-emotional training program (EmCo), with empathic listening practiced for the first 5 weeks and compassionate listening for the second 5 weeks. The pilot demonstrated high compliance with daily practice and yielded promising preliminary evidence for reductions in psychological vulnerability. However, the study lacked both an active control group and a reliable waitlist control group to account for retest and seasonal effects. In addition, the 10-week intervention length proved difficult to implement within the German school calendar due to longer holiday breaks. Thus, the present Edu:Social School Study 2 will employ the same intervention program, the empathy-compassion Dyad training program (EmCo) but with a shorter duration of 8 instead of 10 weeks only, that is school teachers will be systematically taught to distinguish between empathic listening and how to regulate empathy now in the first 4 weeks and learn how to listen compassionately in the second 4 weeks of the Affect-Dyad online training already tested in the CovSocial project (Godara et al., 2021). Typical MBI’s such as MBSR or MBCT (Kabat Zinn, 1982; 2003; Teasdale et al., 2000), are usually 8 weeks long and thus easier to implement in practical fields such as education or healthcare. Furthermore, the Edu:Social School Study 2 will employ mindfulness-based online training (MBT) as an active control group, similar to the one already tested in the CovSocial project (Godara et al., 2021), but this time shortened also to 8 from original 10 weeks. In sum, the first main goal of the present large-scale study is to test the efficacy of an adapted 8-week online empathy-compassion (EmCo) Dyad training program for school teachers. To this end, we designed a three-arm randomized controlled trial including (1) an 8-week mindfulness training program, (2) an 8-week EmCo Dyad intervention, and (3) a waitlist control group that will complete the Dyad training after post-test assessment. To ensure scalability and accessibility, both training programs will be delivered online and via a dedicated study app. A second main goal is to examine the effects of such Dyad intervention within the educational context, with a particular focus on strengthening teacher’s mental health, resilience, thought processes (attention) as well as fostering social emotions and prosocial behaviours. Intervention effects will be assessed across nine primary outcome families, here referred to as domains. Seven domains capture individual-level changes in teachers including 1) mental health, 2) resilience, 3) attention and cognitive processes, 4) social emotions, 5) stress-coping and emotion regulation, 6) listening,

title: Greater Resilience Information Toolkit Japanese Version (GRIT-J)
abstract: The purpose of the present study is to conduct a randomized controlled trial of the behavioral intervention for Japanese nurses, called Greater Resilience Information Toolkit Japanese Version (GRIT-J), to reduce stress and burnout by enhancing resilience. GRIT trains participants to serve as GRIT coaches, who initiate and guide supportive conversations with colleagues experiencing stress or adversity. The GRIT comprises five self-guided modules incorporating psychoeducational videos, written materials, and practical tips. Across modules, the program introduces core concepts related to stress, traumatic stress, resilience, and self-efficacy, as well as principles drawn from Psychological First Aid. The modules collectively present a stepwise framework for initiating supportive communication, recognizing distress, identifying coping strengths, reinforcing existing resources, and encouraging self care. We will recruit 42 Japanese nurses per group (treatment group and comparison group). The treatment group will go through the GRIT program for one month, and the comparison group will be asked to spend time as usual. Stress, burnout, intention to leave, resilience, well-being, social support, coping, and coping self-efficacy will be measured by an online survey before the intervention (baseline) and one month, four months, and seven months after the baseline. We will compare the study variables between the treatment group and comparison group over time. Expected Outcomes of the Study Compared to the comparison group, we hypothesize that the GRIT (intervention) group will show improvements in resilience-related outcomes compared with the comparison group. As a consequence of heightened resilience-related factors, we expect that participants in the intervention group will have lower levels of stress, burnout, and intention to leave and higher levels of well-being than those in the comparison group. Additionally, we will examine the role of resilience-related factors in reducing stress-related factors. We expect that GRIT training will enhance resilience, coping self-efficacy, and social support, which will be further related to reduced stress, burnout, and intention to leave. Conversely, heightened initial stress and burnout are related to lower resilience, coping self-efficacy, and social support, which further result in higher stress and burnout in the long term.

title: Promoting Mental Health in Small Business Leaders: A Randomized Controlled Study in France
abstract: This research project investigates how structured psychological advice can promote mental health and positive behavioral change among manager-owners of small to medium enterprises (SMEs) in France. The study is a randomized controlled trial evaluating two types of scalable interventions: a one-on-one coaching session with a licensed occupational psychologist, and a structured group webinar covering similar content, with the same occupational psychologist. Both formats focus on promoting simple, evidence-based behaviors linked to improved well-being: sufficient sleep, breathing and relaxation practices (e.g., meditation), setting aside personal time, and healthy eating habits. Participants will be recruited in collaboration with local chapters of the CPME (Confédération des Petites et Moyennes Entreprises) and randomly assigned to an intervention or control group. The data collection will take place between Fall 2025 and Spring 2026 and the interventions will be delivered in the Winter 2025-2026. Data will be collected via online questionnaires at three time points (baseline, midline, and endpoint). The study will follow a randomized experimental design involving manager-owners of very small and small-to-medium enterprises (VSEs and SMEs). Participants will be randomly assigned to one of several groups after the baseline questionnaire (Fall 2025). Intervention groups * Control Group (C): No intervention before Q3. As a token of appreciation, participants in this group will be offered access to the Collective Well-Being Webinar after the final survey. * Individual Well-Being Coaching (I): A one-on-one, semi-structured session with an occupational psychologist, held between Q1 and Q2. The session will focus on practical behavioral strategies tailored to each participant’s context. * Collective Well-Being Webinar (W): Participation in a structured online group session held between Q1 and Q2, covering the same behavioral strategies. Content of the interventions Both interventions are designed and delivered by a registered occupational psychologist. They aim to raise awareness, share strategies, and support positive behavior change around four key domains: 1. Sleep 2. Breathing and relaxation (including meditation) 3. Personal time (non-work, non-family) 4. Nutrition Participants in the individual format will receive a follow-up email with tailored resources if applicable. All participants will receive a general summary email with practical tools after the final survey. Data collection Data will be collected via validated, non-clinical scales at three points: * Q1: October 2025 * Q2: January 2026 * Q3: April 2026 The measures include: * WHO-5 (subjective well-being) * BMS-10 (burnout scale) * Life satisfaction * Behavioral indicators using the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), applied to each domain (sleep, breathing, personal time, and nutrition) * Quantitative self-reports of the four behaviors * Demographic questions (age group, gender, company size) collected at Q1, with an opt-out option Primary outcomes include subjective well-being (WHO-5), burnout (BMS-10), self-reported life satisfaction, and behavioral indicators based on the TPB. We expect both interventions to improve well-being over time, with potential differences in effectiveness between the individual and group formats.

title: Beyond Nature Videos: Evaluating BioMusic Breaks for Burnt-Out Nonprofit Workers as a Workplace Restoration Intervention
abstract: Exposure to nature has been shown to positively impact individuals at work, primarily via attention restoration, emotional modulation, and fatigue mitigation. The biophilia hypothesis explains that natural settings replenish depleted attentional resources, foster positive emotions, and reduce fatigue. However, physical access to nature is not always possible during a 9-to-5 workday, especially in urban office settings, so virtual nature interventions such as watching videos and listening to sounds of natural environments have emerged as promising alternatives. Recently, “biomusic”, a new type of virtual biophilia experience, has garnered public interest. To create biomusic, an artist attaches sensors to a plant, which converts the plant’s biodata into sound in real-time, via a process called biosonification, resulting in pitch messages that play musical instruments listeners can enjoy Listening to biomusic while watching the accompanying video of the plant may, like other forms of nature exposure, have positive impacts; however, to date, no controlled experimental study has examined whether biomusic has restorative effects comparable to or superior to traditional (i.e., sounds, pictures, and/or videos of nature) virtual nature breaks. Being able to take restorative virtual nature breaks is important for employees in high-demand jobs where burnout is common. Nonprofit employees frequently work with limited resources, emotionally taxing tasks, heavy workloads, and little support. Indeed, burnout is a pervasive organizational challenge across the nonprofit industry and is linked to employee psychological and physical well-being as well as to workplace attitudes and outcomes. Indeed, almost all nonprofit leaders are concerned about burnout, a large majority are approaching or experiencing it, and about half of workplace shortages are caused by it. Nonprofit workers could benefit from nature breaks during work, but many work in underserved or urban areas without outdoor nature access, neighborhoods where going outside alone is unsafe, or simply in geographies where year-round outdoor access is limited. Thus, accessible and inexpensive biophilic interventions used over time may be a practical long-term strategy to combat, and perhaps prevent, burnout in this population. Moreover, those already experiencing high levels of burnout may benefit more from these virtual nature breaks than those experiencing lower levels of burnout. In the present study, we explore how different types of 10-minute breaks taken during work time impact full-time, nonprofit employees primarily working in person. We also investigate how workers’ baseline levels of burnout may moderate the effects of work breaks. Up to 534 non-profit full-time workers in the United States who regularly use fitness wearables (e.g., Apple Watch, Garmin, Oura Ring, Fitbit) will be recruited via the Prolific research platform and undergo rigorous quality checks. The study will employ a randomized between-subjects experimental design in which participants are randomly assigned to one of three virtual break conditions: 1) A video of natural landscapes with accompanying nature sounds, 2) a video of biomusic with accompanying visuals showing the technology hooked up to the plants, and 3) a video of a standard office break room with ambient office noise, similar to what workers experience when taking a break at their desk, to control for the effect of taking a break independent of nature or biomusic. After completing informed consent, participants complete pre-test measures via an online Qualtrics survey of state and long-term burnout, attention, affect, stress, fatigue, and HR (as captured by their fitness wearable device). Next, participants are randomly assigned to one of the three 10-minute break conditions. After the break, participants complete post-test measures of attention, affect, stress, state burnout, fatigue, and HR. Participants will also report demographics. Data are analyzed with separate 2 (Time: pre-break, post-break) X 3 (condition: traditional nature, biomusic, control) repeated-measures ANOVA (one for each outcome measure: state burnout, fatigue, affect, stress, attention, and HR) to determine how biomusic compares with other forms of work breaks. Additionally, we conduct moderation analyses to further examine whether long-term burnout moderates the effect of break condition on each outcome measure. Our study makes important contributions to the literature regarding workplace nature breaks. First, it provides the first experimental comparison of biomusic to traditional virtual nature breaks. By comparing biomusic breaks to other conditions, namely traditional virtual nature breaks and a control with office ambient noise, the study distinguishes the effects of biomusic from other traditional nature stimuli. Second, by using both self-report survey measures and objective HR measures pre- and post-break, the study offers a robust evaluation of the impact of virtual breaks. Third, by examining burnout as a moderator, we shed light on for whom the virtual breaks have the most positive impact. Together, this research advances understanding of an accessible, virtual biophilic experience that a high-demand population can use to promote attentional restoration, emotional modulation, and fatigue recovery. The study also provides evidence-based insights for organizations seeking scalable virtual interventions to benefit their employees.

title: Improving Teacher Wellbeing: A Randomized Pilot Study of an Online Self-Guided Single Session Consultation Intervention
abstract: Teaching is a stressful job, that often presents with limited time and high job demands. However, the vast majority of the interventions tailored to help mitigate this stress and increase wellbeing are very time consuming and not tailored to meet the specific needs of teachers. To address this gap, this paper utilizes a randomized study design and pilots an online-self guided single session consultation (OSG-SSC) intervention aimed at improving wellbeing. Specifically, in a sample of 122 teachers (intervention group, n = 61; wait-list control group, n = 61) the fidelity, acceptability, and effectiveness of the OSG-SSC across a variety of indicators (i.e., teacher self-efficacy, school connectedness, positive emotions, hope, and burnout) was examined. The results suggests that the OSG-SSC was implemented with a high level of fidelity and found to be a useful and acceptable intervention by teachers. In addition, the OSG-SSC was also found to significantly reduce one aspect of burnout, emotional exhaustion with a large effect.
